II. THE DFA’S APPLICATION OF THE OTHER STATE
TAX CREDIT IS CONTRARY TO ARK. CODE ANN. §
26-51-504, INCOMPATIBLE WITH THE CURRENT
ARKANSAS INCOME TAX REGIME[Footnote 1
stated, “Arkansas Income Tax Act of 1929 (§26-51-
101 et seq.), as amended.], AND CONTRADICTS
OTHER ARGUMENTS ADVANCED BY THE DFA AT
THE ADMINISTRATIVE HEARING.
A. THE DFA’S APPLICATION OF THE OTHER STATE
TAX CREDIT IS CONTRARY TO ARK. CODE ANN. §
26-51-504.
In all but one of the ETAs, Mr. Melson states, "You can not
take a deduction for gambling losses and a tax credit for taxes
paid to other states on the winnings." This statement is wrong
both factually and legally. Factually, the Taxpayer did not take a
tax credit for "taxes paid to other states on the winnings." The
Taxpayer took a tax credit for the taxes he paid to on
account of his gambling activity in . The amount of
taxes owed in took account of the Taxpayers total
income and deductions and calculated his tax obligation
accordingly. This amount, however, was not limited to taxes paid
on his winnings, but rather was a calculation based on income and
deductions on account of his activity in , which is
exactly how Arkansas calculates taxes for its non-residents.
Legally, the limitation on not taking a "deduction for gambling
losses and a tax credit for taxes paid" is not found in Ark. Code
Ann. § 26-51-504(a)(1) or Arkansas Individual Income Tax
Regulation § 1.26-51-504(a). Therefore, Mr. Melson 's statement
in the ETAs must be rejected.
When applying a tax statute, it must be construed most
strongly against the taxing power. See Ragland v. Quality School
Plan, Inc., 279 Ark. 256, 651 S.W.2d 447 (1983). Furthermore, tax
statutes are to be strictly construed in favor of the taxpayer, and
38

matters not appearing in the statute are not to be read into it. See
Morley v. Pitts, 217 Ark. 755,233 S.W.2d 539 (1950). In Morley,
the taxpayer deducted his losses incurred in drilling dry wells
outside the state of Arkansas. The Commissioner of Revenues for
the State of Arkansas (the ''Commissioner") denied the deductibility
of the expenses, claiming that the Act[Footnote 2 stated that, “As
provided previously, the predecessor to Arkansas Code
Annotated § 26-51-504, was codified from Act 162 of 1943 (the
"Act"). The Act is captioned as: ‘AN ACT to Prevent Double
State Income Taxation of Individual Residents of Arkansas.
Section 1 of the Act provides that when the gross income of an
Arkansas resident includes income derived from property
outside the State or business transacted outside the State, the
Arkansas tax shall be first computed as if all the income were
derived from inside the State; and then a credit shall be given
for the amount of income tax owed by the Arkansas resident to
the State or Territory from which such income has been
received by the taxpayer.’” (Emphasis added)] necessarily
implied that deductions are not to be allowed on losses incurred in
business ventures engaged in outside the State. The taxpayer
challenged the Commissioner's finding, the Chancery Court found
for the taxpayer and the Commissioner appealed. In affirming the
Chancery Court, the Supreme Court noted that the Act does not
mention or attempt to change the statute regarding deductible
items. Instead, "[the Act] is concerned with income and not with
deductions. The purpose of the Act, as stated in the caption, was to
protect an Arkansas resident from double payment of income tax."
Morley, 217 Ark. at 757. The DFA argues that Morley is
inapplicable because the DFA did not deny the deduction for
gambling losses. However, Morley is applicable here because the
DFA is claiming that you cannot take a deduction and a credit
related to the same income (as shown by Mr. Nelson's statement in
his ETAs). This is precisely the issue that Morley held was
inaccurate and that a deduction and credit could be taken
concurrently.
Like its predecessor, Ark. Code Ann.§ 26-51-504(a)(1) is not
concerned with deductions. During his direct examination in the
administrative hearing, Mr. Melson acknowledged that the plain
language of Arkansas Individual Income Tax Regulation § 1.26-51-
504(a), which is exclusively relied on by Mr. Melson in the ETAs,
does not contain or support his statement that "You can not take a
deduction for gambling losses and a tax credit for taxes paid to
other states on the winnings." Thus, like the Commissioner in
Morley, Mr. Melson has read into the regulation a limitation that
does not exist: a prohibition of the Other State Tax Credit when a
taxpayer has deductions for gambling losses. Therefore, as was
39

found in Morley, the disallowance of the credit is erroneous
because the limitation imposed by the DFA is not contained in Ark.
Code Ann. § 26-51-504 or in Arkansas Individual Income Tax
Regulation § 1.26-51-504(a).
In an attempt to justify his position, Mr. Melson stated during
the administrative hearing that the Taxpayer's sourced
income from his gambling winnings is completely offset by a
deduction for his gambling losses, and, therefore, the Taxpayer did
not pay any additional tax to Arkansas on his gambling winnings.
Authority for this position by Mr. Melson is also not found in Ark.
Code Ann. § 26-51-504 or in Arkansas Individual Income Tax
Regulation § 1.26-51-504(a). Furthermore, as shown below, this
position is inconsistent with Arkansas' current method of
calculating individual income tax.
Neither Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51-504 nor Arkansas Individual
Income Tax Regulation § 1.26-51-504(a) require netting the items
of out-of-state gross income with the items of out-of-state
deductions to determine the net taxable income and tax owed on
only those out-of-state items. This netting the items of out-of-state
gross income with the items of out-of-state deductions is precisely
the step (hereinafter referred to as the "DFA's Netting Step") that
DFA is now asking this Office to read into Arkansas law. If the
Arkansas General Assembly had intended for this type of
calculation to be made with regard to the Other State Tax Credit,
then it would have provided for this type of calculation in Ark. Code
Ann. § 26-51-504. Instead, the last sentence of paragraph (a)(1)
reads: "However, credit shall not exceed what the tax would be on
the outside income, if added to the Arkansas income, and
calculated at Arkansas income tax rates." The addition of the clause
"if added to the Arkansas income" shows the Arkansas General
Assembly's intent to limit the credit to the total tax liability in
Arkansas, (i.e. on outside income and Arkansas income), so as to
prevent a credit in excess of the tax owed (resulting in a tax refund).
When the DFA interpreted Ark. Code Ann.§ 26-51-504 in
Tax Regulation § 1.26-51-504(a), it clearly agreed with this reading
of the clause and added the following limitation to Arkansas
Regulation § 1.26-51-504(a): "Any credit given shall not be allowed
to exceed what the tax would be on all the Arkansas resident's
income, from wherever derived, if such tax was calculated
using Arkansas income tax rates." During the administrative
hearing, Mr. Melson acknowledged that the limitation in the
regulation was intended to prevent a credit in excess of the tax
owed. However, Mr. Melson maintained that the limitation in the
statute was aimed at limiting the credit to the tax owed in Arkansas
40

on the net outside income. The plain language of the statute does
not support this position. Furthermore, Mr. Melson was unable to
offer an explanation at the hearing as to why the limitation in the
statute was not found in the regulation or why the limitation in the
regulation differed from the limitation in the statute. Clearly, Mr.
Melson's feigned ignorance at the hearing was to avoid
acknowledging that the statute and the regulation are consistent
with one another: both limit the credit to the taxpayer's total
Arkansas tax liability and neither limit the credit to the tax owed on
solely the net outside income. Therefore, the DFA's interpretation
of the Other State Tax Credit is contrary to Ark Code Ann. § 26-51-
504 and is improper.
B. THE DFA'S APPLICATION OF THE OTHER
STATE TAX CREDIT IS INCOMPATIBLE WITH
THE CURRENT ARKANSAS INCOME TAX
REGIME.
There is no justification in Arkansas law for netting specific
items of an Arkansas resident taxpayer's individual gross income
with specific items of deductions to determine the net taxable
income and tax owed by the resident as to only those items.
Instead, an Arkansas resident individual taxpayer first calculates
total income by adding together every item of gross income
(without regard to source). See Ark. Code Ann.§ 26-51-404 and
Form AR1000F, line 21 (a blank AR1000F is attached as Exhibit
A). Then, gross income is adjusted by certain deductions to arrive
at the taxpayer's adjusted gross income. See Ark. Code Ann.§ 26-
51-403 and Form AR1000F, line 23. Then, the taxpayer adds
together every item of deduction (without regard to source) and
nets this amount against adjusted gross income to arrive at net
taxable income. See Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51- 403 and Form
AR1000F, lines 25 and 26. The tax owed is then calculated by
applying the Arkansas tax table to the net taxable income. See Ark.
Code Ann.§ 26-51-201 and Form AR1000F, line 27.
The amount of the deduction for gambling losses under Ark.
Code Ann. § 26-51-424 is a function of the amount of gambling
winnings. However, the deductions for gambling losses are
subtracted from gross income (i.e., the income before deductions
are subtracted) along with other deductions to determine the
taxable "net income", which has no identifiable source. Only then,
tax is calculated on the "net income", if any. The drafters of Ark.
Code Ann. § 26-51-504 clearly understood that taxable "net
income" does not have identifiable sources. Thus, instead of
requiring taxable "net income" to include income from property or
business outside the state, the statute requires "gross income" to
41

include income from these identifiable "gross income" sources. The
DFA's attempt to calculate tax on specific items of "gross income"
for purposes of the Other State Tax Credit is incompatible with the
current Arkansas income tax regime, which calculates Arkansas
individual resident income tax on "net income" without regard to
source.
C. THE DFA'S APPLICATION OF THE OTHER
STATE TAX CREDIT CONTRADICTS OTHER
ARGUMENTS ADVANCED BY THE DFA AT
THE ADMINISTRATIVE HEARING.
During the administrative hearing, Mr. Melson also argued
several times that the Taxpayer paid no tax on his gambling
winnings to Arkansas. He based this claim solely on the fact that
Arkansas allows a deduction for gambling losses to the extent of
gambling winnings and the Taxpayer's losses equaled or exceeded
his winnings in the years at issue. At the hearing, Mr. Melson also
repeatedly stated that the tax paid to was solely on the
gambling winnings because would not have jurisdiction
to tax Arkansas income. Similarly, in the DFA's opening Brief, they
cite Walters v. State of Oklahoma ex rel. Oklahoma and stated that
the "Court determined that the non-Oklahoma income of a non-
resident is used to calculate the Oklahoma income tax rate imposed
on the Oklahoma source income earned by that non-resident, but the
non-Oklahoma income is not taxed." However, Walters v. State of
Oklahoma ex rel. Oklahoma, is a case to determine the
constitutionality of the non-resident income tax system implemented
in Oklahoma. This opinion is not authority that can be relied upon
in Arkansas. Even if it was, the mechanics of the non-resident
income tax calculation were not at issue at that case. The Court's
statement about what was being taxed is dicta based on a statement
provided by the Tax Commission about the general applicability of
the non-resident income tax system and was not the holding of the
case.
However, here, for tax years 2013 through 2017, ,
like Arkansas, allowed a deduction for gambling losses to the extent
of gambling winnings and the Taxpayer still paid taxes to
despite gambling income being the Taxpayer's only taxable activity
that occurred in . When the Taxpayer's representatives
pointed this out, Mr. Melson responded by stating that the reason
the Taxpayer owed tax to on his gambling winnings
despite the deduction for gambling losses (making the gambling
winnings equal $0) was a function of the way that
calculates nonresident income tax. This explanation is
unpersuasive, however, considering that in determining tax liability
42

for non-residents, considers all the Taxpayer's income.
And for some years at issue, the Taxpayer's taxable
income exceed his gambling winnings. See Figure B.
In determining the rate at which nonresidents' income is
taxed, most states consider only the income that is taxable by the
state. A growing number of states, however, including
and Arkansas, determine nonresidents' tax liability by reference to
the nonresidents' total income, wherever earned. Thus, both
and Arkansas considered all of the Taxpayer's income,
from wherever earned, in arriving at the tax owed to each respective
state for the years at issue. Similarly, for 2013 through 2017, both
states allowed a deduction for gambling losses to the extent of
gambling winnings. The DFA offered no explanation as to how the
taxes paid to were solely on the gambling winnings, yet
no taxes paid to Arkansas are attributable to gambling winnings,
when both states offered the same offsetting deduction for
gambling losses. Since the DFA offered no explanation for these
contradictory positions advanced by the DFA at the hearing and in
its opening brief, these positions cannot be relied on to disallow the
Other State Tax Credit.
III. THE TAXPAYER WOULD BE SUBJECTED TO
DOUBLE TAXATION IF THE DISALLOWANCE OF THE
OTHER STATE TAX CREDIT IS NOT REINSTATED.
Although "double taxation" is not mentioned in the language
of Ark. Code Ann.§ 26-51-504, the legislative intent behind the
Act[Footnote 3 stated, “See note 2.”], the predecessor to Ark. Code
Ann. § 26-51-504, was clearly to prevent double taxation of
Arkansas residents. Arkansas Individual Income Tax Regulation §
1.26-51-504(a) contains an additional requirement not found in the
statute: "No credit shall be allowed against the resident's Arkansas
income tax liability unless the resident can clearly show that he or
she would be subject to double taxation on a portion of his or
her income unless the credit is allowed." It is worth noting that a
plain reading of the language of this requirement does not demand
the Taxpayer show double taxation of any specific source, amount
or type of income. Instead, this additional limitation only requires
the Taxpayer to show "a portion of his or her income," not a portion
of his or her source income, is subject to double taxation in order
for the credit to be allowed. This was confirmed by Mr. Melson
during the administrative hearing. Furthermore, this additional
limitation does not change the amount of the credit that is
otherwise allowed. Thus, if a taxpayer is able to show a portion of
his or her income is subject to double taxation, the credit would be
equal to the lesser of taxes actually owed to such other state(s) or the
43

total tax liability in Arkansas. Since the Taxpayer can clearly show a
portion of his income is subject to double taxation, the full amount of
the credits claimed on the Taxpayer's Forms AR1000F (equal to the
amounts in the fourth column of Figure B, above) must be
reinstated.
Arkansas and each take into consideration the
Taxpayer's total income from all sources in determining the taxes
owed to the state. In this way, the Taxpayer's total income is
subject to tax in each state in which they earned income. In order
to ensure taxpayers are not subject to double taxation,
applies a percentage to the net taxable income of nonresidents
reflecting the percentage of total income earned in the state. (Note:
Arkansas applies this same method for determining taxes owed by
nonresidents to Arkansas). However, no limiting percentage is
applied to the income of Arkansas residents who earn income and
pay taxes to other states (i.e., Arkansas taxes its residents on 100%
of their income wherever derived). Instead, Arkansas residents are
entitled to the Other State Tax Credit to ensure they are not subject
to double taxation on any portion of their income.
In this matter, double taxation is demonstrated in the
following table. The second column represents the Taxpayer's total
state income tax liability if his gambling activities partially occurred
in and the credit is disallowed in Arkansas. The third
column represents the Taxpayer’s total state income tax liability if
his gambling activities only occurred in Arkansas. The fourth
column is the difference.
Year
This table shows that the Taxpayer is paying $ more
in state income taxes on the exact same amount of total
income simply because the Taxpayer chose to gamble in
. Keep in mind that, except in 2018, both Arkansas and
allowed the Taxpayer a deduction for gambling losses
that fully offset his gambling winnings (such that, under the DFA's
analysis, his net taxable gambling winnings in both states are $0).
Thus, this $ difference cannot be explained by a difference
44

in the states' taxing methods relating to gambling. Furthermore, in
each year at issue, income tax rates are lower than
Arkansas' income tax rates. Thus, this $ difference cannot
be explained away by a difference in the states' tax rates. The only
plausible explanation is that both states are taxing some portion of
the same income. This fact, which was admitted by Mr. Melson
during the administrative hearing, conclusively demonstrates that the
Taxpayer is subject to double taxation unless the Other State Tax
Credit is allowed.
IV. THE DFA'S RELIANCE ON LAWS FROM OTHER
STATES IS UNPERSUASIVE AND SHOULD BE
DISREGARDED.
As previously stated, the only question to be decided in this
matter is whether the Taxpayer's application of the Other State Tax
Credit was justified under Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51-504. This
question hinges on the interpretation of the following language:
"However, the credit shall not exceed what the tax would be on the
outside income, if added to the Arkansas income, and calculated at
Arkansas income tax rates." The introduction to the Arkansas
Individual Income Tax Regulations (Regulation 1997-4) states:
Pursuant to the authority vested in the Commissioner of
Revenues and in compliance with Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-
301 and § 26-51-104, the Commissioner of Revenues of the
Department of Finance and Administration, with the
approval of the Governor, does hereby promulgate the
following rules and regulations for the enforcement and
administration of Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51- 101 et seq.
PURPOSE OF THE REGULATIONS: The following
regulations are promulgated to implement and clarify the
Arkansas Income Tax Act of 1929 (§ 26-51-101 et seq.), as
amended. All persons affected by or relying upon these
regulations are advised to read them in their entirety, as the
meaning of the provisions of one regulation may depend
upon the provisions contained in another regulation.
Thus, the DFA promulgated Income Tax Regulation § 1.26-51-
504(a) for the exact purpose of clarifying Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51-
504(a).
Tax Regulation § 1.26-51-504(a) is the only authority cited
authority in the ETAs for disallowing the Other State Tax Credit, yet
it is not cited or relied on at all by the DFA in its opening brief.
Perhaps this glaring omission reveals that the DFA has taken a
45

position contrary to Income Tax Regulation§ 1.26-51-504(a).
Regardless, pursuant to the plain language of the regulation, the
credit is limited to the Taxpayer's total Arkansas tax liability,
regardless of source. The DFA, by avoiding the language of the
regulation, is attempting to ignore its own regulation that interprets
the statute in question, and, instead, is attempting to adopt a new
interpretation that would limit the credit to the taxes paid to
Arkansas solely on the other state source income. This new
interpretation is based on the DFA's newly invented method of
calculation that includes the DFA's Netting Step that is first
mentioned in Paragraph II.A above.
However, the DFA fails to cite a single source of precedential
authority to support its new interpretation of Ark. Code Ann. § 26-
51-504(a) and the resulting method of calculation. Instead, the
DFA cites a tax treatise analyzing the laws of states other than
Arkansas and cases from Oklahoma and New Jersey. This
nonbinding authority does not override the DFA's own
interpretation from Income Tax Regulation § 1.26-51-504(a) and
such authority is not binding on this Office. Furthermore, the DFA's
reliance on case law from other jurisdictions and secondary sources
analyzing the laws of other states is unpersuasive as the DFA failed
to argue why such authority should apply to the instant case instead
of applying the applicable regulation that the DFA promulgated.
Obviously, the DFA does not like the results provided by the current
Arkansas laws applicable here.
Mere citation of another jurisdiction's authority is not
singularly persuasive to prove that the State of Arkansas should
interpret a case similarly. Brown v. Arkansas Dep't of Correction,
339 Ark. 458 (1999) (citing Rockefeller v. Rockefeller, 980 S.W.2d
255 (1998)). The sheer numbers of decisions of other jurisdictions
one way or the other on any given question are not controlling on
Arkansas courts. Chamberlin v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co.,
343 Ark. 392, at 398 (2001) (quoting Clampit v. State Farm Mut.
Auto. Ins. Co., 828 S.W.2d 593 (1992)).
In Chamberlin, the Arkansas Supreme Court stated:
Appellant's reliance on authority from other jurisdictions
is equally unpersuasive. Not only is the cited case law not
controlling on this court but, in many cases, it is clearly
distinguishable. Other states' decisions turned upon
specific language in the state's statute authorizing
stacking or an expressed legislative intent favoring
stacking.
46

Chamberlin, 343 Ark. at 398. Like the authority cited by the
appellant in Chamberlin, the authority cited by the DFA is clearly
distinguishable. The treatise and the case law cited by the DFA
each analyze the specific statutory and regulatory language from
other states that have implemented their own version of the other
state tax credit. Since the specific language found in these states'
statutes differs from the language of the Arkansas statute, the
interpretation of the language of such other state statutes by a
foreign court or by a secondary source cannot lend itself to the
interpretation of an Arkansas statute with completely different
language.
For example, in its opening brief, the DFA cites heavily to
¶20.10 of the third edition of the state tax treatise entitled "State
Taxation" by Jerome R. Hellerstein and Walter Hellerstein. See
Hellerstein & Hellerstein, State Taxation, ¶ 20.10, at 20-81 (3rd ed.
2003). This tax treatise summarizes and analyzes state statutory,
regulatory and case law related to state taxation, and ¶20.10
discussed state laws relating to credits for taxes paid to other states.
Unfortunately for the DFA, the authors do not summarize, analyze,
cite to, or even mention Arkansas law at any point in the sixty plus
pages spent on this topic. Nonetheless, the DFA insists that the
limitation found in Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51-504 is the Arkansas
General Assembly's attempt to codify one of the methods
mentioned in the treatise. Specifically, this method is summarized
as "Determining the difference between the resident tax calculated
by first including and then excluding the income subject to tax in
both states." Id. (Emphasis added). As an example of state law
employing this method, the authors of the treatise cite to Hawaii
statutory and regulatory law. The Hawaii statute allowing a credit
for taxes paid to other states and the Hawaii regulations provide the
end result that the DFA wishes would be the end result in Arkansas.
However, the Hawaii statute clearly limits the credit to the amount
of taxes paid to Hawaii solely on the other state income.
Furthermore, the Hawaii regulation clearly provides a step-by-step
method of calculating this intended limitation. However, in
Arkansas, the legislature and the DFA in its promulgation of its
regulation have taken a different approach in the calculation of the
Arkansas other state tax credit. Therefore, the tax treatise cited by
the DFA offers no value in interpreting the Arkansas law that is
applicable here.
Similarly, the DFA cites Stiber v. Director, Division of
Taxation, a New Jersey case that involves the Court interpreting
New Jersey's statute regarding New Jersey's other state tax credit.
9 N.J. Tax 623 (1988). Although DFA cherry picked select language
that seems to support its interpretation of Arkansas law, the DFA
47

failed to explain how New Jersey actually calculates its out of state
tax credit. Attached as Exhibit B is Tax Topic Bulletin GIT-3W that
was prepared by the New Jersey Division of Taxation to assist its
taxpayers in calculating the New Jersey's other state tax credit. The
limitation for the New Jersey credit is found on page 4 of the GIT-
3W and is expressed as a formula:
(a) income actually taxed by both New Jersey and the other
jurisdiction divided by
(b) the income subject to tax by New Jersey and apply that
resulting percentage to
(c) the tax calculated on the total New Jersey taxable
income.
While the actual formula is not relevant to the facts of this matter
since the New Jersey law is different than Arkansas' law, the inputs
to the formula will show, despite DFA's portrayal of the facts of
Stiber, that even New Jersey law does not support the DFA's
attempt to require the DFA's Netting Step in order to determine the
allowable amount of the Arkansas credit. To this end, see pages 5
and 8 of the attached Exhibit B that show both the numerator (a)
and the denominator (b) from the above formula take into account
income before taking deductions. The DFA's argument is that an
Arkansas taxpayer must take into account income after taking
deductions in the calculation of the Arkansas other state tax credit.
Thus, the DFA's own cited authority does not support the DFA's
Netting Step or its denial of the Other State Tax Credit.
Further, as quoted by the DFA, “[t]he objective of the above-
quoted statutory provisions was to avoid the double taxation of the
same income by providing a credit against New Jersey gross income
tax for tax paid to another jurisdiction on the same income . . .
Here, the issue involves the effect on the credit when New York
based income is taxed by New York State and not by New Jersey."
Stiber at 626 (emphasis added). The outcome in Stiber did not
result in a double taxation of the same income because the portion
of the credit disallowed in Stiber was not representative of income
which was taxed in both the other state and New Jersey. Here, the
credit the DFA is trying to disallow does represent income taxed in
both and Arkansas. Therefore, disallowing the credit in
Arkansas does result in the double taxation of the same income,
which as the DFA quotes from Stiber, is the objective of allowing
the credit.
Here, there is no need to resort to secondary sources or case
laws from other states. It is evident from a plain reading of the
Arkansas statute and regulation what limitation on the credit the
48

Arkansas General Assembly and the DFA intended. The Arkansas
Generally Assembly clearly intended to limit the credit to what the
tax would be on all the Arkansas resident's income, from wherever
derived. The DFA provides, in its own Arkansas Individual Income
Tax Regulation § 1.26-51-504(a), that this is the correct
interpretation of the statute. Therefore, the case law from other
jurisdictions and secondary sources cited by the DFA should be
disregarded. Instead, the words of Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51-504
should be given their plain and ordinary meaning as interpreted by
Income Tax Regulation § 1.26-51-504(a), both of which support the
Taxpayer's calculation of the Other State Tax Credit.
V. THE DFA'S INCONSISTENT TREATMENT OF
RESIDENTS AND NONRESIDENTS RESULTS IN A
WINDFALL FOR THE STATE OF ARKANSAS.
On the one hand, the DFA's wants to apply the Other State
Tax Credit in a manner that requires resident taxpayers to take
particular items of out-of-state gross income and net those with
particular items of out-of-state deductions in order to determine
the taxable "net income" from the other state and then apply a tax
rate only to that ''net income" for purposes of the Other State Tax
Credit. On the other hand, Arkansas requires nonresidents to
determine their Arkansas income tax liability, which is the same
method employed by , by reference to their total income,
wherever earned. This tax liability is then reduced by the ratio of
the nonresident's adjusted gross income from sources within the
state to the nonresident's total adjusted gross income. See Form AR
1000NR, Lines 38A - 38D, (a blank Form AR 1000NR is attached
as Exhibit C).
The result is a more favorable calculation for Arkansas in that
it often produces a higher tax liability than if the state looked only
to the nonresidents' taxable income from sources within the state.
This state-favoring result is perfectly exemplified by the facts of the
matter at hand. If the Taxpayer had been an resident
whose only income in Arkansas was gambling winnings that were

Individual Income Tax Assessments and Adjustments
The State of Arkansas imposes an income tax upon “the entire income of
every resident, individual, trust, or estate. The tax shall be levied, collected, and
paid annually upon the entire net income as defined and computed in this
chapter at the following rates . . ..” See Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51-201(a) (Supp.
2017). “Gross income” includes “[g]ains, profits, and income derived from any
67

source whatever[.]” See Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51-404(a)(1)(E) (Supp. 2017). “Net
income” is derived from adjusting gross income by any allowed deductions. See
Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51-403 (Repl. 2012).
Tax deductions and credits, like tax exemptions, exist as a matter of
legislative grace. See Cook, Commissioner of Revenue v. Walters Dry Good
Company, 212 Ark. 485, 206 S.W.2d 742 (1947); and Kansas City Southern Ry.
Co. v. Pledger, 301 Ark. 564, 785 S.W.2d 462 (1990). A taxpayer claiming a
deduction or credit bears the burden of proving that it is entitled to the deduction
or credit by bringing herself or himself clearly within the terms and conditions
imposed by the statute that contains the deduction or credit. See Weiss v.
American Honda Finance Corp., 360 Ark. 208, 200 S.W.3d 381 (2004).
Initially, it must be determined if the Arkansas Supreme Court has issued
an opinion interpreting the provisions of Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51-504(a)(1) which
would be controlling precedent given the facts of this case. The Taxpayer’s
reliance on the holding in Morley v. Pitts, supra, is misplaced (See Brief of
Taxpayer – P. 8 – 10). The Office of Hearings and Appeals has previously issued
decisions which determined that holding in Morley v. Pitts, supra, is not
controlling authority in cases involving the proper calculation of other state tax
credit.
Ultimately, the resolution of this case depends on a determination of
whether the Department correctly adjusted the Taxpayer’s income tax returns for
the relevant tax years. The Department’s adjustments of the Taxpayer’s income
tax returns were based upon its interpretation of the provisions of Ark. Code Ann.
§ 26-51-504(a)(1) (Repl. 2012). The interpretation of statutes by an
68

administrative agency, while not conclusive, is highly persuasive. Aluminum Co.
of America v. Weiss, 329 Ark. 225, 946 S.W.2d 695 (1997). An administrative
agency’s interpretation of a statute or its own rules will not be overruled unless it
is clearly wrong. Arkansas Dep’t. of Human Servs. v. Hillsboro Manor Nursing,
304 Ark. 476, 803 S.W.2d 891 (1991). The Arkansas Supreme Court has
recognized that administrative agencies are often required to interpret statutes
and rules. Walnut Grove School Distr. No. 6 of Boone County v. County Board of
Education, 204 Ark. 354, 162 S.W.2d 64 (1942).
In McCourt Mfg. Corp. v. Rycroft, 2009 Ark. 332, 322 S.W. 3d 491, the
Arkansas Supreme Court discussed a rule of statutory construction which
provides that courts should strive to reconcile statutory provisions relating to the
same subject to make them sensible, consistent, and harmonious. Applying that
rule of statutory construction to the provisions of Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51-
504(a)(1) (Repl. 2012), it is obvious that the second sentence of the subdivision
operates to limit the credit provided in the first sentence of the subdivision.
Accordingly, after consideration of the extensive arguments and citations
contained in the post-hearing briefs and the evidence presented by the parties, a
preponderance of the evidence supports a finding that the Department’s
interpretation of Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51-504(a)(1) (Repl. 2012) (“If the Arkansas
income tax due on the outside income, when added to the Arkansas income, is $0
there is no credit available for taxes paid on that income to another state.” See
Department’s Response to Brief of Taxpayer – P. 10) is not clearly wrong.
The Department has statutory authority to “[a]udit and properly
determine and compute the state tax payable by any taxpayer subject to taxation
69

under any state law”16 and to “employ proper and reasonable audit methods.”17
The greater weight of evidence in the record supports a finding that the audit
methods employed by the Tax Auditor were reasonable and that the Taxpayer
was not subjected to double taxation on his income within Arkansas.18
While the Taxpayer demonstrated that the earning of the income within
resulted in an increased total tax liability for the Taxpayer (when all
state taxes are added), the Taxpayer has not clearly shown that the increase in
total tax was the due to double taxation as opposed to differing state tax policies.
See Income Tax Regulation § 1.26-51-504(a). Consequently, the Department
correctly assessed tax against the Taxpayer (and properly denied the refund
claim) for the years in the audit period.19
Interest was properly assessed upon the tax deficiencies for the use of the
State’s tax dollars. See Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-508 (Repl. 2012). No penalty was
assessed against the Taxpayer.
